title: An AI function for SQL, one row at a time: the answers come back as new columns
excerpt: In January 2025 I put an LLM inside a SQL editor. The answer was text. This is the implementation on top of the Pyodide foundation: the function, the working code and the demo.
text:
In January 2025 I put an LLM inside a SQL editor. MotherDuck's prompt() function inspired it, and it worked. The answer was text.

In the last few weeks, since Jev from TypeSafe AI was released, I have used it for a few small jobs. It is a model that writes no text and answers typed questions with a score or a pick from a list.

My last post covered the foundation: Python and DuckDB running in the web browser with Pyodide. This one is the implementation on top of it: the function, the working code and the same demo. https://lnkd.in/eNz6zPVD

The idea is simple. Take any normal query. Wrap it with the function. Each row goes to Jev in one call, and that one call carries several questions at once: is this personal data, which kind, does GDPR apply, does HIPAA apply. The answers come back as new columns, sitting next to the original ones. Same rows, same columns, plus the answers.

Because the answers are typed, a score or a pick from a list, SQL can filter, join and count them as they are. There is no text to parse.

You can also write your own questions, and each question can name the column it is about: is the name a real full name, is the date of birth plausible, what kind of contact detail is this. They still travel in one call per row.

What happens to a value afterwards, keep, mask, hash, drop or review, is not a model answer. It is a plain rule in code. Doubt goes to review, never to a silent keep.

This is part of my Adaptive Data Governance series. The AI design is System One: the model answers typed questions fast, writes no text, and plain code decides what happens next.

The details are in the RefCard attached: the architecture on page 1, the vocabulary and the eleven built-in answers on page 2, the two ways to call it, the policy table and the guard rails on page 3.

title: Python in the browser, with Pyodide: the foundation for AI in SQL
excerpt: I wanted to show AI in SQL, using Jev. For that I needed Python running next to DuckDB, in a place anyone can open without installing anything. Pyodide gave me that.
text:
I wanted to show AI in SQL, using Jev. For that I needed Python running next to DuckDB, in a place anyone can open without installing anything. Pyodide gave me that.

Pyodide is Python compiled to WebAssembly, so it runs inside the web browser. This post is the foundation: what runs in the web browser, and why each piece is there. The detailed post on the AI function itself is on the way.

What runs in the web browser:

🔵 Pyodide, with Python 3.14, running in a Web Worker so the page stays responsive.
🔵 DuckDB, which Pyodide ships as a package, along with NumPy, pyyaml and pyodide-http.
🔵 An in-memory file system. The browser downloads the CSV or Parquet file and writes it there, so DuckDB reads it from memory. The file is never uploaded.
🔵 Custom Python code, written into the same file system and used like a normal package. One function in it is attached to DuckDB, so SQL can call it.
🔵 Jev, a model from TypeSafe AI that answers typed questions and writes no text. The function sends it each row, and the answers come back as new columns. The model's API does not accept calls from a browser, so a small proxy sits in between. You bring your own key.

title: Jev in job-pilot: typed decisions in my open source job search agent
excerpt: My open source job agent now asks Jev (TypeSafe AI) for its fuzzy decisions, and the dataset it publishes every day stays open.
text:
My open source job agent now asks Jev (TypeSafe AI) for its fuzzy decisions, and the dataset it publishes every day stays open.

job-agents is a small open-source job search tool I built and still maintain: job-scout collects postings from about 95 tech companies' public job APIs into DuckDB, job-matcher scores a candidate's resume against a posting, and job-pilot sits between them and decides which postings are worth scoring.

job-pilot's decisions were string rules. A list of cities decided if a posting was in the US. On one day that rule alone dropped 148 of 308 new postings, some of them good jobs in cities not on the list.

Those three decisions now go to Jev from TypeSafe AI. Jev does not write text. It answers typed questions. job-pilot sends the public facts of a posting and three questions in one call: two of type choice (location bucket, which configured resume variant to score) and one of type noul, a 0 to 1 answer to "is this a target role". Back comes a choice and a confidence. If Jev is unsure or the call fails, the old rule decides. It sees six public fields of the posting, never the candidate's documents.

I left the project open source as a playground, and I keep maintaining it. The dataset it publishes every day is public, and other people query it. I feel responsible for keeping that working.

text:
Today was my last working day at Pentaho.

Eleven years. Three acquisitions. Four names. One product.

My journey with this product began in 2015 at Rokitt Inc., a small New Jersey startup building a machine-learning-driven data discovery product called ASTRA. I was part of the founding engineering team, and the team filed several patents around that technology.

May 2017 — Io-Tahoe, a Centrica plc subsidiary, acquired Rokitt's assets. We re-engineered the product as Halo.

June 2021 — Hitachi Vantara acquired Io-Tahoe. Halo came together with Waterline Data (which Hitachi Vantara had acquired in 2020) to become the Lumada Data Catalog.

November 2023 — with the Pentaho+ platform launch, it became Pentaho Data Catalog, sitting alongside Pentaho Data Integration (PDI) and Pentaho Business Analytics (PBA), products with a 20-year history.

June 2026 — Pentaho found a new home under LEO Software Group, part of Constellation Software.

Through those years I wore many hats. Core engineering first. Then implementation architecture and consulting for enterprises in pharma, life sciences, banking, insurance, government, telecom, and mortgage. In recent years, managing and mentoring engineers across the US, UK, Portugal, Ukraine, and India, with peers from many countries on a follow-the-sun model. Together we set up new competencies from the ground up — performance engineering, SDET, and within it a new AI Engineering practice. Through every role, I never stopped coding.

To the leaders (CTO / CEO / VP of Engineering) I reported to — Rohit Mahajan, Ajay Vohora, Lester Waters, Venkat Subramanian, and Jeff Gierlach — thank you for trusting me at every stage. In hard times, personal and professional, my managers stood by me. I will not forget that.

To my teams and peers — you did the real work, and learning from you was the best part of my job. To our customers — thank you for letting us learn on your hardest data problems.

Pentaho's data intelligence and integration platform is used by 73% of the Fortune 100. The product and the people are in good hands. I will be cheering from outside.

From next week, something completely different: my team changes from people to AI agents — I will be building and managing a fleet of them, in the insurance and underwriting world, a domain brand new to me. After six years of working from home, it is also back to the office five days a week. Real whiteboards, real markers.

Starting over after an eleven-year journey with one product is a little scary. That is exactly why I am doing it.

This is not a sad goodbye — with gratitude, I bid adieu.

See you on the other side.

title: Every enterprise system remembers what happened
excerpt: Very few can explain how it happened. Life sciences shows this gap at its sharpest. A clinical trial runs for years — protocols change, sites join, subjects enroll, adverse events…
text:
Every enterprise system remembers what happened. Very few can explain how it happened.

Life sciences shows this gap at its sharpest. A clinical trial runs for years — protocols change, sites join, subjects enroll, adverse events get reported, approvals pile up. The transactional system holds the current state. The warehouse holds the numbers. But the story — who changed what, why, and what it affected — sits scattered across audit logs.

My new white paper (attached) proposes a third layer: a Semantic and Temporal Knowledge Graph. It connects people, entities, and events, stamps every relationship with valid-from / valid-to time, and stays current by listening to business events.

On top sits Agentic AI Analytics: a supervisor agent that owns no data tools, routing each question to bounded specialist agents — one for governed metrics, one for graph traversals, one for operational state — everything read-only.

Life sciences has been my long-standing interest, and I build in the open there. This paper is the design; the three-part open-source build series comes next, using Graphiti by Zep and FalkorDB.

If clinical trials, knowledge graphs, or agentic AI are your world, it is a 10-minute read. Tell me where the design breaks.

I created my own digital brain as a knowledge graph, and it is already up and running on my laptop/server using Zep’s Graphiti + FalkorDB.

I was inspired by Garry Tan’s GBrain project, but I took a very different approach and it is not just documents, embeddings, or vector search. It connects people, projects, decisions, preferences, events, requirements, procedures, topics and activities — and keeps those relationships updated over time.

The important part for me is temporal memory.

🟦 What I believed earlier.
🟦 What changed.
🟦 Why I made a decision.
🟦 What worked.
🟦 What did not.
🟦 And how I normally approach a problem.

Now, whenever I start new work in claude code cli, my tools can first search the graph for:

🟫 What do I already know about this?
🟫 Have I solved something similar before?
🟫 How did I approach it?

And this is not limited to technical work. The graph can continuously build context from all my activities, decisions and learning — becoming a digital twin of how I work, think and approach problems.

Graphiti handles the temporal knowledge graph. FalkorDB stores the connected memory. My tools recall it when I work.

The idea is simply to connect metrics → risk → decision, rather than looking at an evaluation score in isolation. The RefCard also shows how HARD/SOFT rules can turn metrics into an actual release gate.

text:
I don't open VSCode anymore. Everything I build now runs through the CLI.

I've been living in the terminal since February. I picked up GitHub Copilot CLI but in April this year, I switched to Claude Code — no regrets since.

A few things that changed how I work:

🟦 Claude Code on the iOS app, with remote control enabled on my Mac mini — 64GB, and it's my dev machine and server both.
🟦 Voice prompting when I don't feel like typing (I call myself a power vibe coder.)
🟦 For the past few months I've mostly been building developer tools, skills, rules, and standards, and automating as much as I can with agents — from simple skill-file agents to Python agents where I'm trying out different frameworks.
🟦 Evals, documentation, and what I'd call AI-DLC (AI-assisted development lifecycle, not the AWS product with the same name) are there from day one — shift-left, not added later.
🟦 Observability isn't new to me, but with agents it's stopped being optional. I run Arize and a local OpenObserve setup.

At this point Claude Code writes 100% of the code . I steer — hand it tasks and specs almost round the clock, follow-the-sun style — and my git commit history, how often and when I commit, is the actual record of that.

Most of what I build this way is open and sits outside my day job. The time it frees up goes back into reading tech books/articles, publishing posts/articles, research and listening tech talks — mainly to get sharper at architecture, design, decision-making, planning, spotting the right use cases, and designing test data.

By my own rough read, my output is close to 8x what it used to be — I don't have hard numbers to back that, just how the days feel. What I can say for sure: my interest in coding has grown right along with it, and I'll now pick up any language, because the only thing that matters is whatever fits the problem.

I am a big fan of Boris Cherny (Head of Claude Code at Anthropic) — I follow nearly all his podcast appearances and YouTube talks. His latest conversation on Lenny's Podcast left one line stuck in my head:

"Coding is largely solved. I imagine a world where everyone is able to program — anyone can just build software, anytime."

Boris is not saying it for shock value. He says it plainly, like it is simply where things are heading in the next few months — "for every codebase, every tech stack."

What struck me more is what he said about his own team. Some people specialize in code. Others spend more time on coordination, planning, forecasting, and stakeholder alignment. His bet: by end of year, the title "software engineer" blurs into just "builder." Everyone codes a bit. Everyone does a bit of PM work too.

I don't take this as a threat. I take it as a bell — not to panic, but to prepare.
If the coding part keeps getting commoditized, the edge moves to everything around it:

🟦 Knowing your domain
🟦 Working with SMEs
🟦 Framing the right problem
🟦 Running the project
🟦 Keeping stakeholders aligned. That part does not get automated away so easily.

title: Pairwise Testing deserves more attention—especially now
excerpt: The applied mathematics behind it offers a practical answer to a persistent engineering problem: How do we evaluate a complex system systematically when exhaustive testing is too…
text:
Pairwise Testing deserves more attention—especially now. The applied mathematics behind it offers a practical answer to a persistent engineering problem: How do we evaluate a complex system systematically when exhaustive testing is too expensive and time-consuming?

The key concept is a Covering Array—a mathematical construct that transforms thousands of possible combinations into a smaller, systematic set of test cases while ensuring that every pair of input values appears at least once.

In other words:
• Combinatorial Science defines the challenge.
• Covering Arrays provide the mathematical foundation.
• Pairwise Testing turns it into an engineering practice.

I previously explored this approach in detail, with practical examples, in my article on applying Combinatorial Science to enterprise data platforms. The concept is even more relevant in the era of Agentic AI and AI Evals.

An agentic system may vary across models, prompts, tools, datasets, workflows, memory configurations, policies, and runtime conditions. Testing every possible combination quickly becomes impractical.

Evals are also not fully automated. Humans still steer:
• Evaluation scenarios
• Judgments and expected outcomes
• Rubrics and scoring criteria
• Risk thresholds
• Edge cases and failure analysis

Applying combinatorial techniques can help teams design a smaller but more systematic evaluation matrix—reducing model calls, human review effort, cost, and execution time while preserving meaningful interaction coverage.

"Every pair, at least once. That simple principle may become an important foundation for scalable AI evaluation engineering. "

Read the detailed article for the concepts, examples, and enterprise use cases.

text:
Meet DataGov — my new open-source data governance CLI. Written in Rust. Built for agents.

The goal is simple: one binary, with no Python, Java, Node.js, or Docker dependency, that both engineers and AI agents can run reliably.

DataGov is being designed to:

- Inspect CSV and Parquet datasets
- Profile columns
- Parse, format, and transpile SQL across dialects
- Scan for PII
- Run data quality checks
- Generate a normalized JSON governance report

Here are some commands you can use:
- datagov inspect customers.parquet
- datagov profile customers.csv
- datagov sql transpile query.sql --from spark --to duckdb
- datagov pii scan customers.parquet
- datagov report customers.parquet --profile --pii --output report.json

Why am I building it?

Data governance has been my primary focus for years. As agents increasingly handle data engineering tasks, they require governance tools that provide JSON output, stable exit codes, deterministic behavior, and no interactive prompts. I couldn't find a CLI that merged these agent-ready features with effective data governance capabilities, which led me to create this tool.

The guiding principles are:
- Deterministic first
- Local first
- Privacy first

PII detection will rely on rules and parsers instead of LLM guesses, ensuring sensitive values remain masked by default and that data stays on the local machine.

This is just the beginning; it's an early-stage kickoff rather than a finished product announcement. Bolt 1, the CLI foundation and governance report envelope, is complete, and Bolt 2, focused on dataset inspection, is currently underway. The first milestone will encompass inspect, profile, SQL, PII scan, and report functionalities.

Check out the repository at https://lnkd.in/gsuU48M5

text:
Introducing the latest addition to my agent fleet: the youtube-transcriber, now number nine.

What it does: Simply provide a YouTube link, and it returns the full spoken transcript of the audio, not just the captions. This means you get the actual audio transcribed from start to finish.

Why I built it: In conference talks, important figures are often mentioned in passing. Speakers may only mention a statistic once, and then it's lost. Captions can be auto-generated and may miss crucial information or be altered by marketing teams. I wanted a way to make those numbers searchable, with the speaker and timestamp included.

What powers it:
- LangGraph with five nodes: resolve → fetch audio → transcribe → write outputs, featuring a cached-audio branch for repeat runs to skip downloads.
- faster-whisper (distil-large-v3) operates on my machine, not through an API.
- yt-dlp for audio extraction and ffmpeg for normalization.
- Pydantic for state management, tenacity for retries, and optional OpenTelemetry (I am using Arize and LangSmith)

Each run produces four files: a readable transcript with timestamps, a full JSON file with per-segment timings, an SRT file, and a metrics file.

In the first four talks (The Youtube videos, I used for my testing), I processed 67 minutes of audio, generating 10,658 words in about 14 minutes of compute time—roughly 4.5 to 4.9 times faster than real-time, with zero tokens and zero costs, as it operates entirely on my mac-mini.

The other eight agents include: job-scout, job-matcher, job-pilot, api-test-generator, diagram-generator, github-pr-digest, privacy-classifier, and linkedin-cover-generator.

The landscape of agent frameworks is rapidly evolving, with new names appearing every few weeks: OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph, CrewAI, PydanticAI, LangChain, Claude agents, and more. Despite the varying terminologies and abstractions, the underlying execution pattern remains largely consistent.

Currently, there is no single industry-standard agent lifecycle, but a common pattern is emerging that is more beneficial to learn than memorizing the vocabulary of any one framework. Here are the eleven stages, typically in the order they run:

1. User request
2. Context assembly
3. Memory retrieval
4. Knowledge retrieval
5. Planning
6. Tool or skill selection
7. Execution
8. Response generation
9. Evaluation
10. Reflection
11. Optional memory update

It's important to distinguish between evaluation and reflection. Evaluation assesses whether the output met the task requirements, while reflection considers the process and what changes might be needed for future runs (Feedback loop and Agent Training). Additionally, knowledge and memory are distinct; knowledge is derived from documents, databases, and APIs, whereas memory stems from interactions, preferences, and past decisions. Context is built from both for the current request only.

Response generation, which is stage 8 of 11, is the visible part of the process, but it is often mistaken for the entirety of the system.

title: Last week, I requested my linkedin-cover-image agent to utilize a darker…
excerpt: palette for a privacy article, and it executed the task well. However, the next day, when I opened a new session, I found myself repeating the same request. The agent was not at…
text:
Last week, I requested my linkedin-cover-image agent to utilize a darker palette for a privacy article, and it executed the task well. However, the next day, when I opened a new session, I found myself repeating the same request. The agent was not at fault; the application was. It failed to retain what I had taught it.

Most AI agents today can perform tasks, but very few can improve over time. This isn't due to the model's inability to learn, but rather because the application (The agent) does not preserve that learning.

Consider what a single session actually contains:
- Keep the cover image less crowded.
- Use a darker palette for privacy topics.
- Add more whitespace.
- Move the title higher.
- Avoid unnecessary icons.

In many agent applications, these corrections vanish when the session ends, and the next session begins almost from scratch. The missing component is a reflection loop.

Instead of stopping when the task is complete, the application should run one more step: comparing the original request, the generated output, my corrections, and the final accepted result. It should then ask, "What changed during this interaction?" This allows it to differentiate between a one-time instruction and a genuine preference, reusable design rule, or a recurring workflow issue.

The next step is distillation—not model distillation, but condensing a lengthy interaction into a small amount of reusable knowledge. "For privacy-related covers, prefer a darker, minimal, executive style with more whitespace" -> This single line is far more valuable than storing the entire transcript.

Thus, the loop becomes: reflect, distill, ask for confirmation, store as structured memory, and retrieve it next time. No fine-tuning is needed in that process.

There are essentially two loops at play, and conflating them is a mistake. The first is user-level, capturing my preferences—writing style, palette, level of detail, layout—enhancing the agent's performance for me. The second is product-level; if numerous users request the cover generator to reduce clutter, that indicates a need for a new version of the core skill itself.

Memory personalizes the agent, while reflection enhances the system. Repeated feedback evolves the skill. Building the agent is only half the job; teaching it how to improve is the other half.

Agent Engineering is gradually evolving into Memory Engineering, as memory is not merely the full transcript but the distilled knowledge that deserves to persist beyond the session.

Every week, new ideas emerge around AI-SDLC, spec-driven development, agentic engineering, AI evaluations, governance, observability, and AI-native delivery platforms. The engineering side is gradually converging around common practices, methodologies, and supporting ecosystems.

However, AI is also transforming the economics of software delivery. If AI significantly alters delivery speed, team structures, engineering effort, and quality, how should projects be estimated, priced, and valued?

This question extends beyond just business or sales; it is crucial for architects, engineering leaders, pre-sales teams, delivery managers, and consulting organizations. The estimate prepared during pre-sales ultimately becomes the delivery commitment that engineering teams must fulfill.

It appears that while the engineering conversation is becoming increasingly structured, estimation, pricing, value realization, and commercial models are evolving more quietly. Are our commercial practices converging as swiftly as our AI engineering practices?

I am interested in how others are approaching this transition.

Every project needs a website, docs, a blog, and an API reference. I did not want to hand-build that each time, and I do not want my agents to either.

TemplrPress is the publishing station on that line. It is my opinionated, open-source content publishing system — I built it for my own needs first, and now I am giving it to the community. A 15 MB Go binary: markdown in, product website out.

It started in 2021 as Zypress, built on Vue.js/Nuxt.js CMS. Five years of gradual work later, agents can operate it end to end:

- Docs and OpenAPI reference in one place, free.
- PDF export in pure Go — no headless browser.
- A JSON API serving the same content.
- Paste a link in WhatsApp or Slack and it shows a proper preview card.
- /llms.txt plus a committed code map, so agents read the site and the repo without scanning.

Fully open source, MIT license. Built on Golang and NextJS/TypeScript — the UI compiles into the binary, so the server needs no Node, no database, no build step. One config file, one station done. More stations coming.

Recently, while exploring modern AI evaluation frameworks, I had a realization. Initially, the categories seemed like a collection of technical metrics—valuable for testing model behavior, comparing outputs, and enhancing performance. However, the deeper I delved, the more I understood that they represent something much more significant: the dimensions of AI trust.

- Security: Can the system protect sensitive information and resist misuse?
- Safety: Can it reduce harmful, toxic, or biased outcomes?
- Quality: Is the response correct, relevant, grounded, and reliable?
- Conversation: Did the system understand the user and help accomplish the intended task?
- Trajectory: Did the agent choose the right tools, follow the right process, and reach the outcome in a defensible way?

These are not just evaluation metrics; they are measurable signals indicating whether an enterprise should trust an AI system in production. This perspective shifts how we should approach AI engineering.

Data Governance defines what trustworthy data should look like. AI Engineering builds systems that utilize that data. AI Evaluations provide evidence that those systems behave as intended.

Governance without evaluation remains a set of expectations, while evaluation without governance lacks business and regulatory context. AI engineering without either may yield an impressive system, but not necessarily one that an organization can deploy responsibly.

This forms the basis of my thoughts on Adaptive Data Governance: governance, data quality, engineering, risk, and continuous evaluation should not function in isolation. They must create a connected feedback loop that evolves with the data, business, regulations, and the AI system itself.

Trust cannot simply be declared at the end of development; it must be designed, measured, documented, and continuously earned.

Trustworthy AI is not a feature of the model; it is an engineering outcome.

✅ No separate OpenAI subscription

✅ No procurement delays

I am thrilled to announce the launch of my newest open-source endeavor - DuckDB Studio!

Following the warm reception of "DuckDB Data API & Micro ORM," I'm excited to present this extension product "DuckDB Studio", a web-based utility designed to streamline your interaction with DuckDB databases.

DuckDB Studio is crafted for data enthusiasts and Data Engineers, AI/ML Developers, and those eager to dive into database management without the complexity. Give it a spin and see how it transforms your data workflow.

DuckDB Studio on GitHub https://lnkd.in/eEDVDD7a

The online demo comes with two databases "tickit" and "OpenBeersDB"

- Ease of Access: Effortlessly view your databases and tables.
- Enhanced Data Visualization: Navigate through your data in a user-friendly table view, with convenient pagination.
- Flexible SQL Query Execution: Run any SQL query, tailored to your needs.
- 'Prettify' Feature: Beautify your SQL queries with ease, enhancing readability and maintenance.

As of now, the open-source landscape offers limited tools for querying DuckDB, with DBWeaver catering more to professional use. DuckDB Studio fills this gap, providing a versatile, web-based solution.

Looking Ahead:

- Automatic online API docs for newly created tables/entities.
- Incorporation of SQLGlot for
- advanced online query transpile to 20+ data sources
- A robust SQL Query Optimizer, and
- Enhanced data lineage insights with table, column, and projection extraction.

Inspiration for DuckDB Studio was drawn from several notable projects like Drizzle Studio/ORM, RillData, Grafana Query Editor, and SQLglot, aiming to simplify data handling and analysis.
